nodes.description: The regimen recent reports describe as current treatment: the nonsteroidal androgen receptor antagonist bicalutamide with the third-generation aromatase inhibitor anastrozole, both once a day. Testosterone production is not reduced; the drugs block its action at the receptor and its conversion to estradiol. The one prospective trial (BATT, 14 boys, 12 months, single-arm) normalized the ratio of bone age to chronological age, but the change in its primary outcome, growth rate, was small and variable. Gynecomastia was the commonest adverse event. Case reports describe both sustained control over four to five years and treatment failure.

nodes.description: Ketoconazole inhibits cytochrome P450 steroidogenic enzymes, in particular the 17,20-lyase step, and lowers testosterone within a day. Unlike the receptor-blocking regimens it reduces testosterone production, so serum testosterone can be used to follow it. In one five-patient series adult height matched target height; in another, adult height outcome was limited. Escape occurs when central puberty begins, more readily in boys with advanced bone age. One series reported a transient rise in transaminases in one of five boys; one boy on a high dose developed liver and renal failure with pneumonitis that resolved when the drug was stopped.

nodes.description: The original National Institutes of Health regimen: spironolactone as a weak androgen receptor blocker with testolactone, a first-generation aromatase inhibitor. Either drug alone was unsatisfactory; together they returned growth rate and bone maturation to prepubertal values. Followed to adult height with a GnRH agonist added at central puberty, the approach gave adult heights within the normal male range and modestly below midparental height. Later reports use anastrozole or letrozole in place of testolactone, which also cross-reacts in testosterone immunoassays.

nodes.description: Anastrozole or letrozole combined with spironolactone, used where bicalutamide is not chosen. Reports are single cases and one ten-patient series. A literature compilation found better adult height in men who had received an aromatase inhibitor, but stressed that height outcome with or without treatment is unpredictable.
